list.listitem: Febrile seizures are isolated, self limiting, non-epileptic seizures in children (ages 6 months to 5 years) associated with febrile illness. Febrile seizures alone do not lead to motor or cognitive defects. B
Anticonvulsant therapy is not recommended to prevent recurrent febrile seizures. B
Antipyretics are not effective in preventing febrile seizures. B

Lumbar puncture should be performed for any child with signs or symptoms of concern for bacterial meningitis. It should be considered for any child 6-12 months with a febrile seizure whose immunization for Haemophilus influenza type b (Hib) or Streptococcus pneumonia is deficient or unknown. An LP is also an option for children who are pretreated with antibiotics. B
Parents should be educated on the excellent prognosis of febrile seizures and provided with adequate guidance for non-pharmacologic management of these seizures. C
Do not routinely order electroencephalography and neuroimaging (CT, MRI) on neurologically healthy children who have simple febrile seizures.C
Independent predictors of recurrence include age less 18 months, duration of fever less than one hour, family history of febrile seizure, and temperature less than 40 C. B

background.definition: Febrile seizures are non-epileptic seizures that occur in children between the ages of 6 months and 5 years in association with fever more than 100.4ºF (38ºC) and no identifiable signs of CNS infection, severe metabolic disturbance, or known epilepsy. Febrile seizures can be either simple or complex. Simple febrile seizures last for less than 15 minutes, occur only once in a 24-hour period, are generalized, and occur in children with no known neurological problems. Complex febrile seizures (10%-35%) last for more than 15 minutes, and are either focal or recur within the same 24-hour period. Febrile seizure epilepticus is a state of continuous seizure activity that lasts more than 30 minutes or patient has recurrent seizures within a 30 minute period during which the patient does not regain consciousness and return to baseline neurologic state within 30 minutes of onset of seizure.

list.listitem: Febrile seizures are the most common neurological condition of childhood.
2%-5% of children in the United States and western Europe will have a simple febrile seizure by 5 years of age.
The incidence elsewhere in the world varies between 5-10% (India), 8.8% (Japan), and 14% (Guam).
A more recent survey of over 4000 parents in Gothenburg, Sweden (70% response rate) found that 3.7% of children age 4 years had experienced a febrile seizure.
Febrile seizures are the most common cause of seizures among hospitalized children, responsible for 87% in one series.
Febrile seizure epilepticus is estimated to account for 25 to 52% of status epilepticus cases in children.
It is slightly more common in boys than girls (1.4:1 ratio).
Peak incidence is at 18 months of life.
Viral infection (30%-60%). Amoing viral infections rhinoviruses, enteroviruses, adenovirus, influenza A, B viruses, parainfluenza virus, RSV, SARS Cov2, coinfection have been detected.
Unknown (20%-25%).
Otitis media (8%-30%).
Gastroenteritis (2%-4%).
Meningitis (1%-3%).
Genetics also plays an important role. A subset of patients with febrile seizures displays an autosomal dominance inheritance pattern.

Risk factors for developing epilepsy include underlying neurodevelopmental abnormalities, a family history of epilepsy in a first- or second-degree relative and complex febrile seizure (see risk factor table).

The combined measles-mumps-rubella-varicella vaccine is associated with a slightly higher risk of febrile seizure, compared to the varicella vaccine administered separately from the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (NNT = 2300). A systematic review found that this was true during the 5 to 12 days following vaccination in children 10 to 24 months of age, with the highest observed incidence of 2.95%.
Delaying the initial measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (MMR) beyond 12 to 15 months of age is associated with a greater risk of febrile seizure.
The precise mechanism is uncertain, though some evidence indicates that alterations in voltage-gated neuronal sodium ion channels may play a role.
The developing nervous system of children has a lower seizure threshold than adults; immature brain exhibits enhanced neuronal excitability.
An activated cytokine response, low serum ferritin, and low serum zinc have been implicated in the pathophysiology of febrile seizures.

There is a significant association of the interleukin IL-6 (-572, -173, -597) polymorphism, the T allele and the TT genotype with increased susceptibility of febrile seizures, as evidenced in a recent meta analysis .

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Day care attendance (>20 hours a week)
Febrile seizure in first- or second-degree relative
Young age (<18 months) at first febrile seizure
Low temperature (<40°C) at the initial febrile seizure
Duration of fever (shorter duration before seizure = higher rate or recurrence)
Delaying initial measles-mumps-rubella vaccine beyond 12 to 15 months age

list.listitem: Diagnosed clinically, suspect febrile seizure in young children with generalized seizure activity following an acute fever.

Lumbar puncture is recommended for children with signs of intracranial infection or with complex seizures, and should be considered with prior antibiotic use or if 6 to 12 months of age with incomplete or unknown immunization against Hib or Streptococcus pneumonia. C
CT, MRI, and routine laboratory testing are not recommended unless indicated by clinical exam findings. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Child can suddenly become limp because of painful events or shock
Acute and transient confusion associated with a high fever

list.listitem: Typical presentation is generalized seizure activity following an acute fever in the presence of an appropriately anxious parent.
Most simple febrile seizures will have ended by the time the child presents for care.
Details about seizure should include the duration in minutes, the character of the seizure (focal, generalized), and any associated symptoms (e.g. tongue biting, incontinence, fall/injury)
Details about fever should include the fever grade, peak temperature, and the day of the febrile illness. The presence of fever should be confirmed, either by parental history or direct measurement.

Other important elements of the child’s history include: Presence and duration of recent illnesses (particularly, those requiring treatment) Recent immunizations Medication use Recent trauma Postictal symptoms like drowsiness or confusion Past history of developmental delay, or NICU stay.
Family history of epilepsy, or febrile seizures
Physical exam should, in particular, look for evidence of ear infection, meningitis or other serious bacterial exam.
Complex features of seizure (>15 minutes, focal or recurrent within 24-hour period) modestly raises the likelihood of underlying meningitis (LR 1.9; 95% CI 1.3-2.9 CI).
Historical features of meningitis (febrile illness >3 days, vomiting, drowsiness, physician visit in past 48 hours) raise the likelihood of meningitis (LR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2-2.4 CI).

Major clinical signs of meningitis include petechiae, definitive nuchal rigidity, and coma. Minor clinical signs of meningitis include questionable nuchal rigidity, persisting drowsiness, convulsions, and paresis or paralysis on ED exam.
CT, MRI, and routine laboratory testing are not recommended unless indicated by clinical exam findings.

Laboratory tests such as CBC, blood culture, serum chemistry, urinalysis, urine culture, and lumbar puncture should be obtained if signs of a serious bacterial infection are present. In children with isolated simple febrile seizures, a urine culture should be obtained. Otherwise, routine labs are unnecessary.
A fingerstick glucose should be obtained if the child is seizing at the time of presentation. C
EEG is not indicated for simple febrile seizures.

Lumbar puncture (LP) is recommended for children with complex febrile seizures or signs of intracranial infection. Lumbar puncture should be considered for children pretreated with antibiotics or in those 6 to 12 months old with incomplete or uncertain immunity to Hib or Streptococcus pneumoniae. A simple febrile seizure does not usually require routine LP.
Contraindications to LP include signs of raised intracranial pressure, altered consciousness, cardiorespiratory distress, bleeding diathesis, or local skin infection.
Video recording from parents may help distinguish epileptic seizures from non-epileptic movements.

The diagnosis of febrile seizures is clinical. A careful history and physical exam is generally all that is needed to diagnose simple febrile seizure. Imaging, EEG, or an extensive diagnostic evaluation is not generally indicated.

Order urine culture and any other tests to diagnose underlying infection based on clinical exam. Consider LP in children with complex febrile seizure, evidence of meningitis, less than 6 months old, prior antibiotic use, or if 6 to 12 months old with incomplete or uncertain immunization status.

A simple clinical prediction rule assigns 1 point each for age less 18 months, duration of fever less than one hour, family history of febrile seizure, and temperature less than 40 C. The risk of recurrence was 13% if 0 points, 23% if 1 point, 32% if 2 points, 62% if 3 points, and 75% if 4 points.
Most febrile sezires are benign and self-limiting, and the risk of anticonvulsant therapy to treat recurrent simple febrile seizures outweighs the benefits. C
For patients with ongoing seizure at the time of presentation, IV diazepam (0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg q 15 minutes) is recommended. C
Seizures often abort prior to presentation to the hospital. However, if the child is still ictal, assessment of ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) should precede any pharmacologic intervention.
For patients with ongoing seizure, the lateral recumbent position is preferred to prevent aspiration.

For patients with ongoing seizure at the time of presentation, benzodiazepines are the first-line abortive treatment of choice. IV diazepam 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg q 15 minutes up to total dose of 5 mg or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg up to 4 mg is recommended. Rectal diazepam in a single dose of 0.5 mg/kg for children 2 to 5 years old is an option.
In the absence of IV access, midazolam (0.2 to 0.7 mg/kg) can be administered intramuscularly, rectally or intranasally. An intrabuccal formula is also available.

A Cochrane review concluded that diazepam, clozapam, and phenobarbital all reduce the risk of recurrent seizures (RR 0.36 to 0.69 depending on duration of follow-up and drug). However, their routine use is not recommended as these drugs have significant side effects in up to 30% of children.
Rectal administration of diazepam for abortive use at home may be considered in those with an initial prolonged febrile seizure and in those at highest risk of recurrence.
Carbamazepine and phenytoin have not been shown to be effective in preventing recurrent simple febrile seizures.
Antipyretics do not prevent simple febrile seizures following vaccination.

A randomized trial compared 10mg/kg rectal acetaminophen every 6 hours for 24 hours with untreated controls in 423 children age 6 to 60 months with febrile seizure. Febrile seizure recurred less often in the acetaminophen group (9.1% vs 23.5%, p < 0.001, NNT = 7).
The use of inhaled 5% CO2 to abort febrile seizures without adverse effects is currently under study.
The anxiety created by febrile seizures makes it particularly important to offer appropriate reassurance, parental support and education.
Parents and families should be reassured of the natural course of simple febrile seizures.
Provide parents information on how to recognize and respond to seizures at home, and provide first aid management at home.
Admission is recommended for children with febrile seizures who are younger than 18 months, have had recent antibiotic therapy, or have had complex seizures, or have a prolonged postictal period.
Febrile seizure epilepticus is to be differentiated from complex seizures, both warrant further evaluation often times with hospitalization.

Complex seizures are defined as those that are focal, longer than 15 minutes, or occurring more than once within 24 hours. A study of 183 hospitalized children with complex febrile seizure age 6 to 60 months found that 21% received anticonvulsants in the ED, and none had a further seizure during their hospitalization, and only 7 had further seizures during the hospitalization (6 of whom had multiple seizures prior to admission). Thus, children with complex febrile seizure most likely to benefit from hospitalization are those with multiple seizures.
Social factors should also be considered prior to discharge home from the emergency room, such as access to general and specialty medical care and services.

A study found that non-Hispanic White children are more likely to be hospitalized and receive neuroimaging for febrile seizure. It is not clear whether the additional interventions were useful or improved outcomes, or whether they were potentially harmful.
Children with simple febrile seizures are not at increased risk for motor or cognitive deficits. B
Risk of epilepsy following simple febrile seizures is 1.5% to 2.5% (negligibly higher than the population risk for epilepsy). B
Independent predictors of recurrence include age less 18 months, duration of fever less than one hour, family history of febrile seizure, and temperature less than 40 C. B

There is a 25% to 40% risk of recurrence for simple febrile seizures.Approximately 50% of recurrences occur in the first 6 months after the first simple febrile seizure, 75% within 12 months, and 90% within 2 years.
Children who are younger than 1 year at the time of first febrile seizure have a 50% risk of having recurrent febrile seizures.

A study found that 4 risk factors were independent predictors of recurrent febrile seizures: age less than 18 months, a history of febrile seizures in a first degree relative, a low degree of fever while in the ED, and a short duration between fever and seizure.
Children with simple febrile seizures are not at increased risk for motor or cognitive deficits.
Risk of epilepsy following simple febrile seizures is 1.5% to 2.5% (negligibly higher than the population risk for epilepsy).

A simple clinical prediction rule assigns 1 point each for age less 18 months, duration of fever less than one hour, family history of febrile seizure, and temperature less than 40 C. The risk of recurrence was 13% if 0 points, 23% if 1 point, 32% if 2 points, 62% if 3 points, and 75% if 4 points.
A Swedish cohort study of 4 year old children found that the risk of subsequent seizure disorder was 2.5% (4 out of 157) among children with febrile seizure.
Risk of epilepsy following complex febrile seizures is 4.1% to 6.3%.

Febrile seizures have a benign course with spontaneous resolution over time, these do not lead to any neurological or developmental damage unless there is unusual severity and long duration of seizure activity or association with high fever.

A meta-analysis found that febrile seizures were seen in 29% cases of sudden unexplained deaths among toddlers ages 1 year to 4 years, although most had other infectious, sleep position, and neurologic comorbidities.
No routine testing is recommended for simple febrile seizures.

Parents should be counseled regarding the natural history and outcomes of children with febrile seizures. Many parents fear that their child is dying or sustaining irreversible brain damage during the witnessed seizure.
Reassure parents that following a simple febrile seizure, there is no increased risk of death or brain damage.
Parents should be taught how to measure temperature, how to provide a tepid sponge bath, and the correct dosing of antipyretic medication.

For children with parents who exhibit particularly high levels of anxiety, or for those who are at high risk of recurrence, oral diazepam (0.33 mg/kg/dose given three times daily, and used until the child is afebrile for 24 hours) can reduce recurrence of simple febrile seizures.
